docs.title: First deployment
docs.text:
From code/src on the server:

cp .env.example .env              # fill in Cognito, Gemini, DOMAIN
docker compose up -d solr
docker compose exec solr solr create -c memorylane_v2 -d _default
CORE_NAME=memorylane_v2 bash scripts/setup_solr.sh
docker compose up -d --build
curl -s https://<your-domain>/api/health

Before that, point the domain's A records (with and without www.) at the server and open ports 80 and 443. Ports 8000 and 8983 should stay closed.

The repository's code/src/deploy/README.md is the full step-by-step guide. It covers swap, moving data from an older core, the reboot test, and backups with EBS snapshots.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
cd code/src
git pull origin master
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs -f backend

Container logs are capped at 3 files of 10 MB per service. They contain page ids, not the URLs people save or what they search for: query strings are dropped from the access log, and the backend's own requests to Solr and Cognito aren't logged.

docs.title: Schema changes
docs.text:
Solr's automatic field creation is turned off, so a new field has to exist before the backend that writes it is deployed:

Field Added by Then description scripts/add_description_field.sh Pages get one the next time they're saved page_embedding scripts/add_page_embedding_field.sh python -m scripts.backfill_page_vectors gives older pages a page vector (resumable)

Warning

Never run docker compose down -v. It deletes Solr's data, the downloaded models and Caddy's certificates.

docs.title: Moving pages between cores
docs.text:
scripts/reindex.py copies pages from one core into another under a given user id, re-cleaning, re-chunking and re-embedding them. The source core is never modified.

docker compose exec backend python -m scripts.reindex \
  --source-core memorylane --target-core memorylane_v2 --user-id <cognito-sub> [--dry-run]

docs.title: Publishing the documentation
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs and Material, and published to GitHub Pages by hand from the repository root:

pip install mkdocs==1.6.1 mkdocs-material==9.7.7 pymdown-extensions==11.0.1 model2vec==0.10.0
mkdocs gh-deploy --strict

.github/workflows/mkdocs.yml runs the same build (mkdocs build --strict) on every push that changes the docs, so broken links fail the check, but it doesn't publish.

docs.title: Meaning-based search
docs.text:
Besides the theme's keyword search, the search box finds sections by meaning. After each build, hooks/semantic_search.py embeds every section of the docs with Model2Vec potion-base-8M, a small static embedding model distilled from bge-base-en-v1.5, and writes the files to site/assets/semantic/: the model's word pieces and an int8 vector table (about 8 MB in all), and every section's vector. The file names carry a content hash, so browsers re-download them only when they change.

In the browser (docs/assets/javascripts/semantic-*.js), nothing loads with the page. The first time the search box gets focus, the files are fetched. Each query is then split into word pieces exactly as the build did (BERT WordPiece), its vector is the average of their vectors, and it's compared with every section in a few milliseconds; no neural network runs. The best sections are fused with the keyword results by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, as MemoryLane fuses BM25 and vector search, and shown above them. Meaning-only matches with a cosine similarity below 0.35 are left out.

code/src/frontend/src/lib/docsSearch.test.js checks that the browser's tokenizer and vectors match the build's, using a fixture made from the real model.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: All application code is in code/src of the repository. Commands below run from that folder.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10+
  • Apache Solr 9.x (9.7 is the tested version). Solr 8 has no DenseVectorField, so it won't work.
  • Node.js 18+ for the web app
  • Docker (recommended, for Solr, or for the whole stack)
  • Chrome or Chromium for the extension
  • An Amazon Cognito user pool (see Configuration)
  • Optional: a Google Gemini API key for summaries

docs.title: 1. Backend
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/rabeeh18/ucs503p-202627-MemoryLane.git
cd ucs503p-202627-MemoryLane/code/src
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt   # requirements.txt plus the test tools
cp .env.example .env               # Windows: copy .env.example .env

The first start downloads the embedding model (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, about 130 MB) from Hugging Face.

docs.title: 2. Solr
docs.text:
Start Solr 9.7, for example with the project's Compose file:

docker compose up -d solr
docker compose exec solr solr create -c memorylane_v2 -d _default

Then install the schema. The script is idempotent: it checks the Solr version, creates the core if needed, applies the fields, turns off automatic field creation, and finishes with a smoke test (indexing, BM25 with stemming, KNN with a user filter).

CORE_NAME=memorylane_v2 ./scripts/setup_solr.sh      # Linux / macOS
.\scripts\setup_solr.ps1                              # Windows PowerShell

Add --reset (or -Reset) to drop and recreate the core. This deletes its data.

docs.title: 3. Web app
docs.text:
cd frontend
npm install

The web app reads its VITE_* settings from the same .env file in code/src.

docs.title: 4. Extension
docs.text:
chrome://extensions → turn on Developer mode → Load unpacked → choose code/src/extension.

The extension talks to the hosted site by default. To point it at a local backend, change the endpoints in extension/config.js. See Configuration.

docs.title: Evaluation Methodology
docs.text: MemoryLane's retrieval is evaluated on SciFact, a scientific-claim retrieval dataset from the BEIR benchmark, adapted to MemoryLane's data model.

docs.title: Corpus and queries
docs.text:
• 1,000 SciFact abstracts as documents
  • 100 claims as queries
  • 106 relevant documents across 115 query–document pairs (binary relevance)

Each document gets a synthetic URL of the form:

https://scifact.org/doc/{document_id}

The URLs only give each document a unique identity; titles and text come from SciFact. This is a controlled retrieval benchmark, not a live-web crawl.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
The evaluation uses the same code as production:

  • Documents are saved through ingest_page, the same function behind POST /memory, so cleaning, chunking, embedding and indexing are all exercised.
  • Queries go through hybrid_search, the same function behind POST /search.
  • Everything runs under the user id eval, in a separate core (memorylane_eval by default), so benchmark data never mixes with real users.
cd code/src
CORE_NAME=memorylane_eval ./scripts/setup_solr.sh
python -m evaluation.scifact_ingest      # index the 1,000 documents
python -m evaluation.scifact_evaluate    # writes evaluation/scifact_report.json

It doesn't need the live server. A throwaway Solr container works just as well, and it keeps the benchmark off the production machine:

docker run -d --name ml-eval-solr -p 127.0.0.1:8983:8983 solr:9.7
docker exec ml-eval-solr solr create -c memorylane_eval -d _default
CORE_NAME=memorylane_eval ./scripts/setup_solr.sh     # on Windows: scripts/setup_solr.ps1
python -m evaluation.scifact_ingest --solr-base http://localhost:8983/solr
python -m evaluation.scifact_evaluate --solr-base http://localhost:8983/solr
docker rm -f ml-eval-solr                              # when done

Indexing takes about two minutes on a laptop, and the evaluation about three.

docs.title: Configurations compared
docs.text:
Configuration What it uses Hybrid The live search: both retrievers, fused BM25 only Keyword retrieval alone Vector only Meaning (embedding) retrieval alone Hybrid, no relevance floor The live search with MIN_VECTOR_SIMILARITY at 0, so weak vector-only matches are kept Hybrid, no second-chunk bonus The live search with PAGE_SECOND_CHUNK_WEIGHT at 0, so a page is scored by its best chunk alone

Each configuration is a setting patched for that run only. The single-method runs set the other method's weight to 0 (BM25_WEIGHT or VECTOR_WEIGHT), which turns that retriever off completely: it isn't queried and none of its results take part. Until November 2026 a zero weight only zeroed its score, so its pages could still fill empty result slots. Numbers measured before then (the earlier table in Results) may be slightly affected.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
All use binary relevance (an abstract is either a right answer or not), the top 10 results, and URLs compared after normalisation.

Quality

Metric In plain words Hit@1, Hit@3, Hit@10 Share of claims with a right abstract in the first 1, 3 or 10 results MRR@10 How high the first right result is, on average (1 = always first, 0.5 = second on average) Recall@10 Share of all right abstracts that appear in the top ten nDCG@10 How well the right results are ordered, with the top positions counting most MAP@10 Average precision at each right result, so it rewards finding all of them early

Behaviour and speed

Metric In plain words Empty rate Share of claims that got no results at all (what the relevance floor could cause) Average results Results returned per claim, at most 10 Latency p50, p95, mean Search time per claim inside the backend process, in ms: the middle case, the slowest 5%, and the average. Network and sign-in checks aren't included.

Confidence

With 100 claims, a few lucky or unlucky ones move the averages. For Hit@1 and MRR@10 the report gives a 95% bootstrap interval: the claims are resampled with replacement 2,000 times (fixed seed), and the middle 95% of the resulting averages is the range. When two configurations' ranges don't overlap, the difference isn't luck.

Before any timing, every claim is searched once untimed, so the first configuration isn't slowed by cold caches. Each configuration also starts with an empty query-embedding cache. The report (evaluation/scifact_report.json) holds the settings used, every configuration's metrics, and the rank of the first right result for every claim.

docs.title: Second evaluation: your own library
docs.text:
SciFact measures scientific claims, not how people look for pages they've read. The second evaluation runs on a real library, with queries written by its owner: for each page, how they would actually search for it.

Each query has a category, so a change shows up where it should:

Category The query... Example navigational names the page, by its title or what it's called "nav2 behavior trees docs" site names the site it was on "reddit post about rust lifetimes" topic says only what it was about "baking bread with a starter" time says when it was seen "the article on caching from last week"

evaluation/evaluate.py reports Recall@1/3/5/10 and MRR overall and per category, the rank of the expected page for every query, and the queries where it wasn't first. Queries whose expected URL isn't one of the user's saved pages are listed and left out of the metrics. That usually means a URL copied from the browser rather than the one MemoryLane stored, and no ranking change could ever find it.

On the server, with the eval file going in on stdin and the report coming out on stdout (nothing is written inside the container):

cd code/src
# 1. Your user id (page counts per user)
docker compose exec -T backend python -m evaluation.generate_eval --core memorylane_v2 --list-users

# 2. A starting set: a random sample of your pages, queries left empty
docker compose exec -T backend python -m evaluation.generate_eval --core memorylane_v2 \
    --user-id <user id> --starter --limit 50 --out - > evaluation/personal.json

# 3. Fill in each query and category, delete pages you don't remember, then:
docker compose exec -T backend python -m evaluation.evaluate --core memorylane_v2 \
    --user-id <user id> --eval-file - --out - \
    < evaluation/personal.json > evaluation/personal_baseline.json

# 4. After a search change, run step 3 again into personal_report.json and compare
python3 evaluation/compare.py evaluation/personal_baseline.json evaluation/personal_report.json

compare.py needs only the standard library, so it runs on the host. It prints each metric with its change, and every query whose rank went up or down.

A feature behind a setting can be compared without deploying old code, since docker compose exec -e overrides it for that one run. For example, search with and without site, time and URL handling:

docker compose exec -T -e QUERY_INTENT_ENABLED=false backend python -m evaluation.evaluate \
    --core memorylane_v2 --user-id <user id> --eval-file - --out - \
    < evaluation/personal.json > evaluation/personal_off.json
docker compose exec -T backend python -m evaluation.evaluate \
    --core memorylane_v2 --user-id <user id> --eval-file - --out - \
    < evaluation/personal.json > evaluation/personal_on.json
python3 evaluation/compare.py evaluation/personal_off.json evaluation/personal_on.json

docs.title: Results on a development library
docs.text:
Tested on a copy of an early real library: 31 browsed pages from about a dozen sites, among about 1,000 SciFact pages as distractors, with queries written by hand.

Set Search Right page first MRR 35 queries, used while building it before 0.86 0.900 after 0.94 0.971 18 held-out queries before 0.72 0.787 after 0.94 0.944

The held-out set was written after the feature and not tuned on, except for one fix it led to (browsing verbs like look added to the filler words), after which it scores 1.00. Most of the gain is in site queries (held-out MRR 0.75 → 1.00) and time queries (0.38 → 1.00, three queries); topic-only queries don't change, and neither do SciFact's 100 test claims (MRR@10 0.581 either way). Both sets are small, so the numbers on your own library are what count.

evaluation/personal* is git-ignored and kept out of the Docker image, since these files hold real URLs and titles.

Queries made from page titles (generate_eval.py without --starter) are near-certain hits for keyword search, so they say little about precision. The starter set is meant to be written by hand.

docs.title: Evaluation Results
docs.text: These are SciFact results for the current search: bge-small-en-v1.5, 150-word overlapping chunks embedded with the page title, Reciprocal Rank Fusion, the relevance floor, and pages scored by their best chunk. They were measured on 19 November 2026 with evaluation.scifact_evaluate (see Methodology): 100 claims over 999 indexed abstracts. One of the 1,000 abstracts failed to index, and it isn't the answer to any claim.

docs.title: Current search
docs.text:
Configuration Hit@1 Hit@3 Hit@10 MRR@10 Recall@10 nDCG@10 MAP@10 Hybrid (live search) 0.71 0.84 0.93 0.786 0.922 0.810 0.768 BM25 only 0.63 0.76 0.86 0.705 0.837 0.728 0.687 Vector only 0.75 0.86 0.94 0.812 0.932 0.837 0.803 Hybrid, no relevance floor 0.71 0.84 0.93 0.785 0.922 0.810 0.768 Hybrid, old second-chunk bonus (0.3) 0.44 0.73 0.92 0.601 0.897 0.663 0.578

In plain words:

  • Hit@1: how often the right abstract is the very first result. Hit@3 and Hit@10 are the same for the top 3 and the top 10.
  • MRR@10: how high the first right result is, on average. 1.0 means always first; 0.5 means second on average.
  • Recall@10: the share of all right abstracts that appear in the top ten (some claims have more than one).
  • nDCG@10 and MAP@10: how well all the right results are ordered, with mistakes near the top counting most.

No claim got an empty result list in any configuration. Hybrid search took about 75 ms per query in the middle case and 90 ms for the slowest 5% (on a laptop, inside the backend process; network and sign-in checks aren't included).

docs.title: How sure are these numbers?
docs.text:
With only 100 claims, some of the variation is luck. A bootstrap (resampling the claims 2,000 times) gives these 95% ranges:

Configuration Hit@1 MRR@10 Hybrid (live search) 0.62 – 0.79 0.72 – 0.85 BM25 only 0.54 – 0.72 0.63 – 0.78 Vector only 0.67 – 0.83 0.75 – 0.88 Hybrid, old second-chunk bonus (0.3) 0.34 – 0.54 0.53 – 0.68

The old bonus's range doesn't overlap the live search's, so turning it off is a real gain. Hybrid and vector-only overlap almost completely, so the small gap between them may be luck.

docs.title: Scoring a page by its best chunk
docs.text:
Until November 2026, a page's score was its best chunk's score plus 0.3 times its second-best chunk's score (PAGE_SECOND_CHUNK_WEIGHT). This was meant to favour pages that match in more than one place. With Reciprocal Rank Fusion, though, the scores of neighbouring results are very close: rank 1 scores 1/61 and rank 10 scores 1/70. A bonus of 0.3 × 1/62 is bigger than that whole gap, so a longer page with two matching chunks beat a shorter page that matched better. When that search got the first result wrong, the page it put first had 2.1 chunks on average; the right answers had 1.3.

Every bonus size tried made ranking worse:

Bonus Hit@1 MRR@10 nDCG@10 0.3 (before) 0.44 0.601 0.663 0.1 0.56 0.701 0.741 0.05 0.64 0.749 0.783 0.02 0.71 0.786 0.810 0 (now) 0.71 0.786 0.810

So the weight is now 0, and a page is scored by its best-matching chunk alone. The bonus held back BM25-only and vector-only runs just as much: they went from MRR@10 0.414 and 0.455 to 0.705 and 0.812.

docs.title: The relevance floor costs nothing here
docs.text: Turning the floor off changed almost nothing (MRR@10 0.786 → 0.785), and no claim lost all its results. The floor only drops weak vector-only matches, and the right abstract is rarely one of them.

docs.title: Hybrid and vector-only are level on SciFact
docs.text: Vector-only is slightly ahead (MRR@10 0.812 against 0.786), within the margin of error. SciFact claims rarely share exact words with their abstracts, which plays to meaning-based search. Hybrid is kept for everyday searches, where keywords matter: exact names, error messages, product codes and site names, which a meaning-only search can miss. The personal-library evaluation measures those kinds of queries.

docs.title: Earlier pipeline
docs.text:
The numbers published before November 2026 came from the earlier pipeline: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, 300–500-word chunks (so most abstracts were a single chunk, and the second-chunk bonus rarely applied), and min-max score fusion (0.5 / 0.5).

Method MRR@10 Recall@10 nDCG@10 BM25 only 0.648 0.812 0.678 Vector only 0.780 0.887 0.801 Hybrid (min-max fusion) 0.754 0.917 0.789

The current search beats it on every measure. Hybrid: MRR@10 0.786 against 0.754, Recall@10 0.922 against 0.917, nDCG@10 0.810 against 0.789. Vector-only: 0.812, 0.932 and 0.837.

docs.title: Tutorial: Your First Saved Page
docs.text:
This tutorial takes you from nothing to finding a page by describing it. It uses the hosted MemoryLane at memorylane.site, so you only need Chrome (or another Chromium browser). It takes about ten minutes.

You will:

  1. create an account and install the extension,
  2. save a page by hand,
  3. find it by meaning, by exact words, and by site and time,
  4. read a summary, delete a page and undo it,
  5. turn on automatic capture safely.

Once you're done, the Usage Guide covers every feature in detail.

docs.title: 1. Create an account
docs.text:
Open memorylane.site and press Get started. Sign up with Google, or with an email address and a password.

You should see the home page with a search box and the message that your library is empty. Each account has its own private library; nobody else can see or search it.

docs.title: 2. Install the extension
docs.text:
1. Open memorylane.site/extension and download memorylane-extension.zip. Unzip it.
  2. Go to chrome://extensions and turn on Developer mode (top right).
  3. Click Load unpacked and choose the unzipped folder.
  4. Pin MemoryLane to the toolbar (the puzzle-piece menu), open it and press Sign in. Use the same account as on the website.

You should see the popup with the current page and a Remember this page button.

docs.title: 3. Save your first page
docs.text:
Open any article you'd like to keep. For this tutorial, use the Wikipedia article on photosynthesis.

Open the extension and press Remember this page.

You should see "Saved just now" with an Undo button. MemoryLane has extracted the article's text (without menus and footers), split it into passages and indexed them. Back on the website, the page appears under Recently saved.

Save two or three more pages on different topics, so the next steps have something to choose between.

docs.title: 4. Find it by meaning
docs.text:
On the website, type a description that does not use the article's title:

how plants turn sunlight into energy

You should see the photosynthesis article first, with a snippet: the two or three sentences that best match your description, with the matching words highlighted. MemoryLane matched the idea, not the wording.

docs.title: 5. Find it by exact words
docs.text:
Now search for a precise term from the article:

Calvin cycle

Exact names, codes and rare words are found by keyword search, which runs alongside the search by meaning. A page that holds the words you typed is kept even when its meaning is only loosely related.

docs.title: 6. Say where or when
docs.text:
If you remember the site or the time, add it:

wikipedia article i saved today

You should see your Wikipedia pages from today ranked first. Site names come from the sites you've saved from, and times can be words like yesterday, last week or in march. These are hints: a better match from another site still shows up. See Searching.

docs.title: 7. Read a summary
docs.text:
Hover over a result (or select it with the arrow keys) and press Summarise, or press S.

You should see a short summary of that page, written for your query. Summaries are made only when you ask, and only that page is sent to the summary model.

docs.title: 8. Delete a page, and undo it
docs.text:
Open the account menu (your initial, top right) and choose All saved pages. Hover over a page and press the bin icon.

You should see the page disappear and a toast saying "Page deleted · Undo". Press Undo within six seconds and the page comes back. Otherwise it's deleted for good. Closing or reloading the tab in those six seconds still deletes it.

docs.title: 9. Turn on automatic capture
docs.text:
In the extension popup, switch on Auto-capture at the bottom. The first time, the popup explains what it does; confirm to turn it on.

From now on, MemoryLane saves pages you actually read: on screen for 30 seconds, or scrolled halfway through. It only saves pages that look like content, such as articles, documentation, posts and videos. It never saves email, banking, social media, private apps, login or payment pages.

To try it, read an article for half a minute and open the popup.

You should see it under Auto-saved today, with Remove and Never this site. To keep a site out for good, use Excluded sites in the popup. See What automatic capture skips.

docs.title: What you've learned
docs.text:
• Saving is one click, and automatic capture keeps only what you read.
  • You find pages by describing them. Exact words, sites and times help but aren't needed.
  • Everything you save is private to your account and can be deleted at any time.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Usage Guide: every feature in detail, including keyboard shortcuts, YouTube videos and voice search.
  • Privacy: what is stored and what leaves the server.
  • Installation: run your own copy instead of the hosted one.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
This section follows a page from the moment you save it to the moment you find it again.

  • System Overview
  • Capturing Web Content
  • Content Processing
  • Storage

docs.title: Capturing Web Content
docs.text: The Chrome extension is MemoryLane's collection layer. The server does the cleaning.

docs.title: What the extension sends
docs.text:
When you save a page (or auto-capture picks one up), the extension injects content.js into the tab, which returns:

  • The page's full HTML
  • Its visible text (the fallback if cleaning finds nothing)
  • The canonical URL, if the page declares one. After an in-page navigation (single-page apps such as Reddit, YouTube or GitHub change the address without reloading) it's sent only if it describes the current page: same host and path, and each of its parameters matching the address. So watch?v=X is kept on watch?v=X&t=90s, but post A's canonical is dropped while viewing post B. The same rule decides the popup's "Saved" status.

The service worker posts these, with the URL, title and whether the save was manual, to POST /api/memory, using the signed-in user's access token. If the token has expired, the extension refreshes it once and retries.

Auto-capture also checks the page against the capture rules and your excluded sites before sending anything, and doesn't send a URL again while a save of it is in progress, or within a minute of auto-capturing it.

docs.title: A save, end to end
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram

    actor U as User
    participant P as Extension popup
    participant B as Service worker
    participant T as The page's tab
    participant Y as youtube.com
    participant A as FastAPI
    participant S as Solr

    U->>P: Remember this page
    P->>B: save(tab)
    alt YouTube video

docs.title: What the backend does
docs.text:
All of this happens in one function, ingest_page (backend/ingest.py). It is shared by the API, the re-index and backfill scripts and the evaluation.

  1. Take the user id from the verified token (never from the request). Refuse addresses that aren't http or https with 400.
  2. Prefer the canonical URL if it's on the same site and isn't a parent of the page (single-page apps such as Reddit keep a stale one), then normalise it.
  3. Compute page_id = sha256(user_id | normalised URL)[:32]. Drop an unread count from the front of the title ("(3) Reddit" becomes "Reddit").
  4. YouTube: use the transcript, description and details the extension fetched in your browser instead of the page (YouTube blocks the server; see YouTube Videos). A video without captions is saved from its description.
  5. Other pages: extract the main text from the HTML with trafilatura. If that fails, use the extension's text.
  6. Reject the page with 422 if it has fewer than 50 words, and a new page with 403 once the account has reached its page limit (5,000 by default).
  7. If the page is already stored with the same content hash and embedding model, return unchanged and do nothing. An automatic save of a page that's already stored also returns unchanged, even if the text changed a little, so it never moves the page's save date; only a manual save updates a saved page.
  8. Chunk, embed, compute the page vector and description.
  9. Upsert the chunks as {page_id}::{n}, then delete any higher-numbered chunks left from an older, longer version.

The response is {status: saved | unchanged | skipped, message, page}.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text: Because page_id is derived from the normalised URL, the same page saved twice (with or without www., tracking parameters or a fragment) updates one entry instead of creating two. Different users saving the same URL get separate entries.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text: MemoryLane is two pipelines that meet in Solr: one that saves pages and one that finds them. Both run under the signed-in user's id.

docs.title: Saving a page
docs.text:
Page in Chrome (or a YouTube video)
          ↓
Extension: HTML + text + canonical URL
          ↓
Caddy (HTTPS) → FastAPI, with a Cognito access token
          ↓
Verify the token → user_id
          ↓
Normalise the URL → page_id = hash(user_id, URL)
          ↓
Clean (trafilatura) or fetch the transcript
          ↓
At least 50 words? Changed since last save?
          ↓
Chunk (≤150 words, 30-word overlap)
          ↓
Embed "title + chunk" (bge-small-en-v1.5, 384-d)

Solr: chunks + page vector + description

docs.title: Finding it
docs.text:
Query (typed or spoken)
          ↓
Web app → Caddy → FastAPI (token → user_id)
          ↓
   ┌──────────────┬──────────────┐
BM25 (edismax)        Vector KNN (query embedding)

          ↓   both filtered by user_id
Reciprocal Rank Fusion
          ↓
(optional cross-encoder rerank)

Group chunks into pages
          ↓
Relevance floor
          ↓
Snippets → results

docs.title: Separation of responsibilities
docs.text: Part Responsibility Extension Collecting pages, auto-capture rules, excluded sites Web app Search, library, summaries, account Cognito Who the user is Caddy HTTPS, static files, routing /api FastAPI Token checks, ingest, retrieval, summaries Sentence Transformers Embeddings Solr Storage, BM25 and KNN search Gemini Optional summaries Amazon SES Emails problem reports

docs.title: Content Processing
docs.text: Before it is stored, a saved page is cleaned and split into small passages, and each passage is turned into a vector.

docs.title: URL normalisation
docs.text:
The same page can have many URLs. MemoryLane normalises them by:

  • Lower-casing the scheme and host
  • Removing www.
  • Removing fragments (#...)
  • Removing trailing slashes (except the root /)
  • Removing tracking parameters: utm_*, fbclid, gclid, ref, ref_src
  • Sorting the remaining query parameters

The page id is the first 32 hex characters of sha256("{user_id}|{normalised_url}").

docs.title: Cleaning
docs.text:
Raw page text is full of menus, cookie banners, "related articles" lists and footers. MemoryLane runs trafilatura on the page's HTML to keep only the main content. If trafilatura finds fewer than 50 words, the text the extension sent is used instead. Either way, citation markers such as [4] and junk lines (dividers, table rules, icon rows, lone words) are removed and whitespace is tidied. YouTube transcripts skip trafilatura.

Pages with fewer than 50 words after cleaning are rejected.

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
The text is split into paragraphs, then sentences, and packed into chunks:

Rule Value Largest chunk 150 words Overlap each chunk starts with ~30 words of the previous chunk's last sentences Short tail a last chunk with under 40 new words merges into the one before Long sentences hard-split by words

Small, overlapping chunks keep each vector focused on one idea, and the overlap stops an idea being cut in half at a chunk boundary.

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
Each chunk is embedded as title + chunk with:

BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5   (384 dimensions, L2-normalised)

Queries are embedded with BGE's search instruction (Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages:) in front. Passages are embedded without it. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 can be used instead by changing EMBEDDING_MODEL and clearing the prefix.

Embeddings are computed in batches of 32, and the last 1,024 query embeddings are cached.

docs.title: Page vector and description
docs.text:
Two more values are computed per page:

  • Page vector: the normalised mean of the page's chunk vectors. It powers related pages (GET /memory/{page_id}/related).
  • Description: the page's meta description, otherwise its first readable sentences (up to 300 characters). Snippets fall back to it when no sentence matches the query well.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: MemoryLane stores everything in Apache Solr 9.7, in a standalone core named memorylane_v2.

docs.title: Why Solr?
docs.text:
One system covers what MemoryLane needs:

  • Full-text search with BM25, English stemming and stopwords (text_en)
  • Dense-vector KNN search (DenseVectorField, HNSW, cosine) with pre-filtering, so a vector search only ever looks at one user's pages
  • Updates and deletes by query, and cursor-based scans

docs.title: Document model
docs.text:
Each chunk is one Solr document. Chunk 0 also carries the page-level fields.

Field Type Purpose id string {page_id}::{chunk_index} user_id string Owner: the Cognito sub of the first sign-in for that email; every query filters on it page_id string Groups a page's chunks url string Normalised URL domain string Site title text_en Page title (boosted ×2 in search) text text_en Chunk text chunk_id, total_chunks int Position and count timestamp date When the page was saved content_hash string Skips re-processing unchanged pages embedding_model string Re-embeds when the model changes description string, stored only Snippet fallback embedding vector, 384-d, not stored Chunk vector for KNN page_embedding vector, 384-d, stored (chunk 0) Page vector for related pages

scripts/setup_solr.sh is the single source of truth for this schema. Automatic field creation is turned off, so a document with an unknown field is rejected instead of silently adding a guessed field.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Solr holds the pages; two small SQLite files next to it hold sign-in links and problem reports. Solr isn't relational, so the diagram shows the logical model: a library is the user_id that every chunk, link and report carries.

erDiagram
    LIBRARY ||--o{ PAGE : owns
    PAGE ||--|{ CHUNK : "split into"
    LIBRARY ||--o{ SIGN_IN : "reached by"
    LIBRARY ||--o| EMAIL_LINK : "claimed by"
    LIBRARY ||--o{ REPORT : sends

    LIBRARY {
        string user_id PK "Cognito sub of the first sign-in"
    }
    PAGE {
        string page_id PK "sha256(user_id | URL)[:32]"
        string url
        string domain
        string title
        date timestamp
        string content_hash
        string embedding_model
        string description "chunk 0"
        vector page_embedding "384-d, chunk 0"
    }
    CHUNK {
        string id PK "page_id::n"
        string user_id FK
        string page_id FK
        int chunk_id
        int total_chunks
        text text
        vector embedding "384-d, not stored"
    }
    SIGN_IN {
        string sub PK "accounts.db sign_ins"
        string library FK
        string email
        real created_at
    }
    EMAIL_LINK {
        string email PK "accounts.db libraries"
        string library FK
        real created_at
    }
    REPORT {
        int id PK "reports.db reports"
        string user_id FK
        string email
        text message
        text context "JSON"
        real created_at
        real sent_at
        int attempts
        real next_try_at
        text last_error
    }

PAGE isn't a separate document: its fields live on the page's chunks (chunk 0 carries the page-level ones), as the table above shows.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text:
• Saves use commitWithin (1 s) rather than explicit commits.
  • Deleting one page uses a soft commit instead, so a list fetched straight afterwards (the website reloading while the delete is sent) no longer shows it.
  • A re-saved page is upserted chunk by chunk, then any leftover higher-numbered chunks are deleted, so there are never duplicates.
  • Deleting a page deletes by user_id and page_id; deleting an account's data deletes by user_id.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text: Every read, search, delete and scan in backend/solr_client.py adds a user_id filter, and refuses to run if the user id is missing or malformed. Vector searches pass the filter as a KNN pre-filter, so other users' vectors are never considered.

docs.title: Saving Pages
docs.text: Pages get into MemoryLane through the Chrome extension, in one of two ways.

docs.title: Remember this page
docs.text:
Open the extension on any page and press Remember this page.

  • The popup confirms Saved just now, with an Undo button.
  • If the page is already in your library, the popup says so and offers Remove.
  • Saving the same page again updates it. If its text hasn't changed, nothing is re-processed.
  • A page needs at least 50 readable words. Pages with less (an empty app screen, a login form) are refused with a message.

Alt+Shift+M opens the MemoryLane website from anywhere in Chrome.

docs.title: Automatic capture
docs.text:
Automatic capture saves pages you actually read, as long as they look like something worth keeping: an article, documentation, a post or a video. It is off by default: you turn it on in the extension popup, and the first time you do, the popup explains what it does before enabling it.

It only runs while you're signed in. Signing out stops it.

Instead of trying to list every site you wouldn't want saved, it only keeps pages that pass three tests:

  1. The address isn't private: not email, banking, social media, a private app, a local address, or an account area (lists below).
  2. You read it: the page was on screen for 30 seconds, or you scrolled at least halfway down a long page. Pages you bounce off (wrong clicks, redirects, login walls) are never saved.
  3. It reads like content: at least 150 words of readable text that isn't mostly links, and no sign of being a private screen: no visible password field, no compose box or document editor, not mostly a form, and not marked noindex (the tag most logged-in pages carry). Videos pass on their page type.
flowchart LR
    load([Page finishes loading]) --> on{Auto-capture on<br/>and signed in?}
    on -- no --> skip([Not saved])
    on -- yes --> ok{Eligible page, not an<br/>excluded site, not MemoryLane?}
    ok -- no --> skip
    ok -- yes --> read{Read it? 30 s in view,<br/>or scrolled halfway}
    read -- no --> skip
    read -- yes --> recent{Being saved, or auto-captured<br/>in the last minute?}
    recent -- yes --> skip
    recent -- no --> extract[Extract the page:<br/>HTML + text, or a video's captions]
    extract --> content{Reads like content?<br/>no password field, editor, noindex}
    content -- no --> skip
    content -- yes --> post[POST /api/memory]
    post --> server{Server checks<br/>the address again}
    server -- refused --> skip
    server -- ok --> stored([Cleaned, chunked, embedded and<br/>stored under your account])

docs.title: What automatic capture skips
docs.text:
• Social-media sites
  • Banks and payment services
  • Email: Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo Mail, Proton Mail, iCloud Mail and other webmail (including mail. and webmail. sites, and /owa/ and /webmail/ pages)
  • Private apps: Google Docs, Drive, Calendar and Classroom, Microsoft Teams and OneDrive, Notion, Slack, WhatsApp Web, Telegram Web, Figma, Trello, Dropbox, iCloud, chat assistants, cloud consoles, and college systems (Canvas, Blackboard, and moodle., lms., portal. and similar sites)
  • Local and intranet addresses: localhost, 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, .local, .internal
  • Account areas of any site: dashboard, admin, settings, profile, inbox, messages, notifications, cart and orders pages
  • Links that carry a secret, such as ?token=, ?code= or ?session=
  • Login, sign-up, account, password, checkout, billing, payment and wallet pages
  • Browser-internal pages (chrome://, chrome-extension://, file://, ...)
  • Search-engine result pages
  • Utility pages such as error, privacy, terms, cookie and sitemap pages
  • Files: PDF, images, audio and video, archives, CSV, JSON, XML
  • Pages that don't read like content (see the three tests above)
  • YouTube pages that aren't a video, and videos longer than two hours

The server checks the address rules (and noindex) again for every automatic save, so even an outdated extension can't store these pages.

docs.title: Auto-saved today
docs.text:
The popup lists the last few pages automatic capture saved in the past day. Each has Remove, which deletes it, and Never this site, which deletes it and excludes its site, so a page you didn't want is gone in one click. Pages you've since deleted on the website drop off the list when you open the popup.

Automatic capture never touches a page that's already in your library: it keeps the date you saved it, and it doesn't appear in this list. To update a saved page, press Remember this page.

docs.title: Excluded sites
docs.text:
From the popup you can exclude the current site with one click. The extension's options page lists every excluded site, and you can add or remove them there. Excluded sites are never captured automatically, but you can still save a page from them by hand.

Manual saving skips the automatic-capture filters: if you press Remember this page, the page is saved (as long as it has enough text). The button is there whether or not automatic capture is on, so you can still save a page it skipped, such as a Reddit thread or a long video.

docs.title: When a capture fails
docs.text: If an automatic save fails (no connection, or you were signed out), reloading the page tries again. A page isn't sent twice within a minute, and the extension checks the tab is still on the same page when it reads it, so text from one page is never saved under another's address.

docs.title: Recently saved
docs.text: The home page lists your most recently saved pages under the search box. View all opens the full library.

docs.title: All saved pages
docs.text: The library (/library) lists every page you saved, newest first, 20 at a time with Load more. Each row shows the title, site, letter tile and when you saved it.

docs.title: Deleting a page
docs.text:
Use the bin icon on a row in the library, home page or search results (or Shift + Del on a selected search result).

  • The page disappears at once and a toast offers Undo for 6 seconds.
  • After that, it's deleted from the server.
  • If you close or reload the tab during those 6 seconds, the delete is sent straight away, and a reloaded page keeps it hidden.
  • If the server can't delete it, the page comes back with an error message.
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Shown
    Shown --> Hidden: Delete (bin or Shift+Del)
    Hidden --> Shown: Undo within 6 s
    Hidden --> Deleting: 6 s pass, or the tab closes
    Deleting --> Deleted: Server confirms
    Deleting --> Shown: Server error (toast)
    Deleted --> [*]

docs.title: Account menu
docs.text:
The circle at the top right shows your initial and opens the account menu:

Item What it does All saved pages Opens the library Get the extension Opens the extension page (hidden once the extension is installed) Delete all my data Deletes every page you saved, after a confirmation Report a problem Sends a message to the maintainer; the form shows everything sent with it (what's included) Sign out Signs out of the website

Signing out of the website doesn't sign out the extension. Sign out of it from its own popup.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Describe what you remember in the search box on the home page. Press / anywhere on the home page to jump to it.

the article on reducing database query latency

docs about ROS navigation

The query doesn't need the page's exact words. MemoryLane matches by meaning as well as by keywords.

docs.title: Saying where or when
docs.text:
If you remember the site or when you saw it, say so. MemoryLane ranks the pages that fit higher:

You type MemoryLane looks first at reddit post about rust lifetimes your reddit.com pages about rust lifetimes rotten tomatoes reviews of dune your Rotten Tomatoes pages about Dune nvidia docs on cuda graphs your pages from nvidia.com and docs.nvidia.com what i read yesterday pages you saved yesterday, nearest first the article from last week about caching pages saved in the last two weeks about caching recipe videos from 1 september pages saved around 1 September github.com/tokio-rs/axum that saved page, then the site's others

A site counts when it's one you've saved pages from, by its name without www. or the ending (wikipedia, github, nvidia; wiki and yt work too). Times can be today, yesterday, N days/weeks/months ago, this or last week/month/year, recently, a date (31 august, aug 31), a month after in/from (in march), or a year after from or with a word like saved (what I saved in 2025).

These are hints, not filters: a page from another site or time still shows up if it matches better.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Each result shows:

  • The page title, linking to the page
  • The site, with a letter tile for the domain
  • A snippet: two or three sentences from the page that best match your query, with the query words highlighted
  • When you saved it
  • Summarise, for a short summary of that page

Up to 10 pages are shown. Pages that only loosely match your query are left out instead of padding the list, so a short list means nothing else was close enough. If nothing matches, MemoryLane suggests describing the idea rather than exact words.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text: Key Action ↑ ↓ Move between results / Jump to the search box Enter Open the selected page S Show or hide the summary of the selected page Shift + Del Delete the selected page (with undo) Esc Clear the search

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Every search runs a keyword search (BM25) and a meaning search (vector KNN) over your pages at the same time, then combines them. See Retrieval Architecture.

docs.title: Summaries
docs.text:
Each search result has a Summarise button. It asks Google Gemini for a short summary of that one page.

Summarise
   ↓
POST /api/summarize {query, id}
   ↓
Load the page's stored text (your pages only)
   ↓
Gemini
   ↓
Summary shown under the result

docs.title: What Gemini sees
docs.text:
Only the stored text of the page you chose (long pages are truncated), and your query. Gemini is asked to summarise that text only, without adding outside knowledge.

If a page contains instructions meant for the AI ("ignore your rules and …"), they are treated as page text, not commands. A summary never contains a link that isn't on the page itself, and it's shown as plain text. See Security for how this works.

docs.title: Length
docs.text:
The wording of your query sets the length:

  • Short (1–2 sentences): words like brief, quick summary, tl;dr, in a nutshell
  • Long (2–3 short paragraphs): words like detailed, in-depth, comprehensive, explain fully
  • Medium otherwise

docs.title: When it's unavailable
docs.text: Summaries need a Gemini key on the server. Without one, or if Gemini fails, the result shows a short message instead, and search keeps working. GET /health reports whether Gemini is available.

docs.title: Voice Search
docs.text:
In browsers with speech recognition (Chrome and Edge), the search box shows a microphone button.

  1. Press the microphone and allow microphone access if the browser asks.
  2. Say your query.
  3. The recognised text appears in the search box.
  4. Press Enter to search.

Voice input only fills in the search box: the query then goes through the same search as a typed one. Speech recognition is done by the browser, not by MemoryLane.

If the browser has no speech recognition, the microphone button isn't shown.

docs.title: YouTube Videos
docs.text:
A YouTube video page has almost no readable text, so MemoryLane saves the video through its transcript (captions) and its description instead.

youtube.com/watch?v=…, youtu.be/… or youtube.com/live/…
        ↓
Recognise the video id
        ↓
In your browser: fetch the title, channel, length,
description and captions from YouTube
        ↓
Title + channel + length + description + transcript
        ↓
Same pipeline as any page: chunk → embed → store

docs.title: Why your browser fetches the transcript
docs.text:
YouTube blocks transcript requests from cloud servers, and the MemoryLane server runs on AWS. Your browser isn't blocked, so when you save a video the extension fetches its captions and details from YouTube and sends them along with the page.

The extension does this from inside the YouTube tab, because YouTube's API refuses requests that come from an extension directly. It talks only to youtube.com, the same site you are already on, and sends no cookies.

The server only fetches a transcript itself when an older version of the extension sent nothing. It builds the video's URL from the video id and never fetches a URL sent by the browser.

docs.title: What gets stored
docs.text:
• Video title, channel and length
  • The description (its first 2,000 characters)
  • The transcript text: English captions if the video has them (uploaded before auto-generated), otherwise its first caption track in the original language

You then find the video by what was said in it, or by what its description says.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A video with no captions is saved from its title and description, if the description has at least 15 words. With neither, it can't be saved.
  • MemoryLane's search model is trained on English. A transcript in another language is saved as it is (YouTube doesn't translate captions for this kind of request), so search finds such a video mainly through its title and description.
  • Automatic capture skips videos longer than two hours, and skips them when their length can't be determined. Remember this page saves them anyway.
  • YouTube Shorts and YouTube pages that aren't a video (home, channels, search) are never saved.
